title: Lujan v. G & G Fire Sprinklers, Inc. (2001)
shortTitle: Lujan v. G & G Fire Sprinklers, Inc. (2001)
summary: When a state withholds contract payments from a public works subcontractor for suspected labor law violations, an ordinary breach of contract suit in state court is all the process the Due Process Clause requires.
notes:
Key line: "We hold that if California makes ordinary judicial process available to respondent for resolving its contractual dispute, that process is due process." (Rehnquist, C.J.)

Citation: 532 U.S. 189 (2001).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, the California Department of Industrial Relations, and several state officials in their official capacities, including the state Labor Commissioner, whose name gives the case its title. The respondent was G & G Fire Sprinklers, Inc., a fire protection company that installs sprinkler systems and had worked as a subcontractor on several California public works projects. The United States appeared as amicus curiae supporting the state. The dispute arose under provisions of the California Labor Code governing prevailing wages on public works and the withholding of payments when a subcontractor fails to comply.
sections.Material Facts: The California Labor Code required contractors and subcontractors on public works to pay a state determined prevailing wage and keep payroll records. Section 1727 required the awarding body to withhold from the contractor all wages and penalties forfeited under the contract, and section 1729 allowed the contractor to withhold matching sums from the subcontractor. Sections 1731 and 1732 let the contractor or its assignee sue the awarding body for breach of contract to recover the withheld amounts within ninety days of completion. In 1995 the Division determined that G & G, as subcontractor on three public works projects, had failed to pay the prevailing wage and to keep or furnish payroll records. It issued notices directing the awarding bodies to withhold from the contractors amounts equal to the forfeited wages and penalties. The contractors in turn withheld payment from G & G. According to G & G the total withheld exceeded $135,000. No hearing preceded or followed the withholding.
sections.Procedural History: G & G sued the state petitioners under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 in the District Court for the Central District of California, claiming that the withholding notices deprived it of property without due process. The district court granted summary judgment, declared sections 1727, 1730 through 1733, 1775, 1776(g) and 1813 unconstitutional and enjoined enforcement. A divided Ninth Circuit affirmed, 156 F.3d 893 (1998). The Supreme Court vacated and remanded for reconsideration in light of American Manufacturers Mutual Insurance Co. v. Sullivan, 526 U.S. 1061 (1999). On remand the Ninth Circuit reinstated its judgment, again by a divided vote, 204 F.3d 941 (2000), reasoning that the scheme afforded no hearing at all. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 531 U.S. 924 (2000), heard argument on February 26, 2001, and reversed on April 17, 2001.
sections.Issue: Whether the California statutory scheme that authorized the state to direct withholding of payments due a public works subcontractor for suspected violations of the Labor Code, without any administrative hearing before or after the withholding, deprived the subcontractor of property without due process of law in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment, or whether the availability of a breach of contract suit in state court to recover the withheld sums provided constitutionally sufficient process.
sections.Holding: The Court held unanimously that because state law affords G & G sufficient opportunity to pursue its claim for payment under its contracts in state court, the statutory scheme did not deprive it of due process. Assuming without deciding that the withholding was state action and that G & G had a property interest in its claim for payment, the Court concluded that an interest of this kind can be fully protected by an ordinary breach of contract suit. If California makes ordinary judicial process available to resolve the contractual dispute, that process is due process. The judgment of the Ninth Circuit was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Rehnquist distinguished the cases the Ninth Circuit relied on, James Daniel Good Real Property, Barry v. Barchi, FDIC v. Mallen and Sniadach. In each of those the claimant was denied a right by which it was presently entitled to exercise dominion over real or personal property or to pursue a gainful occupation. G & G had been denied no present entitlement. It had been deprived of payment it claimed under a contract, based on the state's determination that it had not complied with the contract's terms, and it held only a claim that it had complied and was entitled to be paid in full. Quoting Cafeteria Workers v. McElroy, the Court repeated that due process is not a technical conception with a fixed content. The Labor Code let the contractor or its assignee sue the awarding body, and G & G conceded at argument that it had sued awarding bodies as an assignee on previous projects. The delay of a lawsuit, while a hardship, does not deprive a party of its claim, since damages are ordinarily awarded only at the end of a suit. Even without an assignment, a common law suit against the contractor appeared available under California law, as J & K Painting Co. v. Bradshaw suggested. As the challenger, G & G bore the burden of showing the scheme unconstitutional and had not shown that this avenue was closed.

topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: The available common-law contract remedy sufficed without a separate administrative hearing in the setting described.
topics.lrs-o-new-property: The Court assumed a contractual right to payment is a property interest but held its nature determines what process is due.

learning.separateOpinions: None. Chief Justice Rehnquist delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court.
